Conclusion This study compares the performance of emerging MPEG-5 EVC and H.266/MPEG-VVC video compression standards with that of their predecessor H.265/MPEG-HEVC. In addition, given the growing popularity of the AV1 video codec, AV1 is included as an alternative baseline. Particularly, it was determined that the coding gain of VVC in terms of BD-BR PSNRYUV is larger than that of EVC, and it is about 40% for encoding 4K/2160p video sequences; however, this comes with a very significant computational complexity increase by a factor of more than 9 compared to HEVC and by a factor of approximately 2 compared to EVC. In turn, EVC achieves bitrate savings of about 30% for 4K/2160p encoding. On the other hand, for encoding FHD/1080p video sequences, VVC achieves bitrate savings of ~37% over HEVC, while the corresponding bitrate savings of EVC are ~23%. Furthermore, when testing the AV1 encoder in a twopass VBR mode, for the 4K/2160p and FHD/1080p encoding, it was found that AV1 provides bitrate savings of ~20% and ~24%, respectively. Based on the extensive experimental results presented in this work for a wide range of resolutions, frame rates, and bit depths, the authors find both EVC and VVC to be very promising successors to HEVC. However, the jury is still out on the speed of their adoption.
